en: Title: *Saṃvarodaya*, Chapter 24 Author: [Scriptural] Source: TUL Matsunami no. 404, folios 66v3–72r1 [Translation of the Tibetan text: Then, the Blessed One, the Great Lord of the Vajra, spoke these words to the assembly of bodhisattvas. “O sons of the Victorious One! Listen well and attend closely. I shall now explain the supreme rite for the accomplishment of all activities, which is the essence of all mantras and the source of all siddhis. First, one should visualize the mandala of the *saṃvara* in the center of a clean place. There, one should draw the maṇḍala with colored powders according to the prescribed proportions. In the center, one should place the image of the Lord of the Vajra. To the east, the consort Vajravārāhī; to the south, the consort Khecarī; to the west, the consort Pātālavāsinī; and to the north, the consort Bhūcarī. In the intermediate directions, one should place the four goddesses: Śabdarūpā, Gandharasā, Sparśarūpā, and Dharmadhātu. Next, one should perform the ritual of the preliminary service (*puraścaraṇa*). Having purified the body, speech, and mind, one should recite the mantra ten million times. Then, having offered the oblation (*bali*) and performed the fire sacrifice (*homa*), one should proceed to the rite of the great accomplishment. One should visualize oneself as the deity, possessing the three secrets, and emanate rays of light from the heart-center. These rays should summon the wisdom-beings (*jñānasattva*) and cause them to enter into union with the commitment-beings (*samayasattva*). By means of this union, one should offer the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five meats (*pañcamāṃsa*) as the inner offering. Furthermore, one should practice the yoga of the winds (*prāṇāyāma*) and the retention of the vital breath. By means of the four mudrās—the great mudrā, the dharma mudrā, the karma mudrā, and the samaya mudrā—one should attain the state of the Vajradhara. This is the secret of all secrets, the most profound of all profundities, and the king of all rites. It should not be revealed to those who lack faith or who have not received initiation. It is the path to liberation for those who possess the proper lineage and are devoted to the *saṃvara*. Thus, the Blessed One, the Great Lord of the Vajra, taught this chapter on the supreme accomplishment of all activities. [End of Chapter 24]
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the arising of the expansion of ritual actions (*karmaprasara*);
these mantras bestow various accomplishments (*siddhi*) and bring about the results of various rites. (24.1)
Oṃ, homage to Mahākāla, who dwells in the cremation ground, together with his followers! It is as follows: Oṃ, move, move forward, dance, cause to dance; O Devaliṅga, svāhā!
Having performed ten thousand services (*sevā*), one should take the *liṅga* at midnight and recite [the mantra] until [the deity] arrives. This is the summoning of the *piṇḍa*.
Oṃ cāmuṇḍe dhūmakeśi vidyujjihve phana 2 paca 2 devadattam ānaya svāhā.

Having drawn Mount Sumeru with red [pigment] on the sole of the left foot, and having inscribed four *hrīḥ* syllables in the four inner corners, one should step upon the central mantra-word and recite it. This is the supreme method for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
OṂ VAJRAKRODHA MAHĀBALA HANA DAHA PACA VIDHVAṂSAYA YO ’SAU MĀRAYA HŪṂ PHAṬ.

Having fashioned a Vāsuki snake one span long from clay of the Vālmīka mound mixed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should sprinkle it with water infused with *karavīra* bark. Having offered incense of *guggulu* continuously and a sacrificial offering (*bali*) of the three white substances, a stream of water falls within seven days. If it does not rain, on the seventh day one should break [the image] into pieces, place them in a jar, and set it adrift upon a river; then they will certainly cause rain. This is the procedure for causing rain. Oṃ gaga ari gaga svāhā.

Having washed one's face with this [mantra] and having empowered a clod of earth by reciting it seven times, one should place it at the entrance of someone’s cave; thus the binding of their mouth is accomplished. *Oṃ mukās tiṣṭhanti mūkāḥ kāḍhyanti (? lāṅgalaṃ mūkānāṃ mūtrapurīṣeṇa devadattasya mukhaṃ bandhāmi svāhā.* One should place the undigested dung of a bull into the cave. In whatever matter involving the binding of a person’s mouth or legal dispute, there is certain success.

Oṃ, homage to Niśābhairava! Cini 2! In the form of a Kirāta, I bind the snouts of the Mukhikas, as well as those of monkeys, rhinoceroses, serpents, bears, wild boars, and so forth. Siri siri, khiri khiri, svāhā! Having recited this mantra twenty-one times over a clod of earth with one hand, one should cast that clod at the four corners of a house, a field, or a garden; thus it becomes free from affliction. 24.7

Alternatively, having combined the substances of poison, salt, black mustard, radish seeds, *dhuttūraka* seeds, or *mahākāla* seeds, and having stirred them with the blood of a buffalo, a pig, and a jackal, one should offer flowers, incense, and a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) on the fourteenth day. Thereafter, grasping [the mixture] with the right hand, one should spend the fourteenth night with the threatening roar of the left index finger. Thus, the binding of the boundary and the enclosure is accomplished. Oṃ hrīṃ brīṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.

Having consecrated cow dung with this mantra, one should throw it into a water reservoir; the curd will perish. If one throws it into milk, one is released. 24.9 Oṃ re! To the Lord of Mantras, the Sovereign of the Three Worlds! Act! Act! Go! Go! Devour! Devour! Eye diseases! Siri! Siri! Destroy! Destroy! Hūṃ phaṭ! Hrī hrī! Svāhā!
The mantra for wiping away eye diseases:
|| 24.10 || Oṃ aruṇe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.

Having consecrated water with mantras, one should wash the eyes; this destroys eye diseases. (24.11) Having made seven pieces from the root of *valā* and bound them on the hand, it destroys fever. By binding the root of *apāmārga*, it destroys quartan fever (*cāturthakajvara*). Taking a piece of wood from the *saptaparṇa* tree, if one holds it at the threshold of the door or on the path, liquor is destroyed. Once it is removed, there is release. (24.12) *Oṃ namo caṇḍāṅkuśa huru 2 svāhā*.
One should fumigate with these— pigeon droppings, the juice of *indragopaka*, collyrium, *guggulu*, cinnamon, *nakha*, *kuṣṭha*, and likewise the seeds of *naga*—
combined with molasses.
This incense shall be for sale with profit from all the wares.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, O Shushkamukhi Chamunde! Ciri miri! Strike down [so-and-so]! Bring [such-and-such a person] under control! Svāhā!
Indrayava, vacā, kuṣṭha, tagara, and likewise mustard seeds,
along with portions of sūkṣmailā, nāgapuṣpa, and resin (sarjarasa)—
a garment fumigated with these quickly undergoes transformation. 24.14

Having formed a casket with two *ya* letters, one should place [the name] in the middle of the *namaḥ*. Having taken a leaf from a tree with upward-pointing leaves, one should write upon its leaves with a crow’s wing as a pen, using poison and black mustard.
Combined with funeral-ground charcoal, the [diagram] should be written and worshipped while well-concealed.
On a Tuesday during the asterism of Aśleṣā, when there is a wind-storm, one should cause it to be carried away by a river;
the enemy will then be driven into exile.

Having gone to a solitary linga at night, for one whose great soul is devoted to the recitation of the mantra: *Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ*—this is the ritual application for eradication (*uccāṭana*). (24.16) Having made an effigy out of fallen cow dung, one should fashion it to be sixteen finger-breadths in size. Having written the name on a cloth from a cemetery and placed it within the belly of that [effigy], one should angrily press its mouth with a lump of grain. One should also wrap it with hair from a corpse. And into its mouth, being enraged, one should strike with blows using a pestle over which the mantra has been recited seven times; thus it becomes paralyzed. (24.17) This is the procedure for subjugation (*vaśa*).

Having smeared a mandala in the northwestern corner and having written the name of Devadatta on a birch-bark leaf, one should place it in the middle of that dough-ball; it will cause a large crow to appear and will drive him away. 24.18.

One should empower a vessel made of clay kneaded by the hands of a potter more than a thousand times and place it in the midst of water while holding one's breath; he becomes as stable as a morsel of food. 24.19.

Now, if one wishes to kill enemies, having made an image out of either beeswax or flour, one should have it well-concealed from the mouth down to the soles of the feet on a cloth stained with decoctions. Placing one's hand upon it and reciting the mantra—interwoven with the victim's name—one thousand minus one times, one should place the image in a corner of a temple. Having pinned its heart with a stake of *khadira* wood and sprinkled it with water from a camel’s hoof-print while reciting the mantra, one should worship it at the three junctions of the day with an angry mind; [the enemy] will perish. 24.20

One should mix [the seeds] smeared with five kinds of mustard and blood, and smeared with the sharp oil of a *snātaka*, with iron powder. Having grasped the name of [the victim] one hundred times, one should offer a thousand oblations. He dies at that very moment.

In the fire of a cremation ground, having stirred *bhallātaka* fruits smeared with red ochre, mustard, and blood with sharp oil, one should offer eight thousand oblations while grasping the name of [the victim] one hundred times. He dies instantly of epilepsy; he vomits blood, or dies from colic or fever.

Having fashioned an image of the enemy with cremation-ground ashes, one should, facing south, step upon it with the left foot and, with disheveled hair and in a state of rage, offer eight thousand oblations while uttering the name of the person [against whom the rite is directed]. That enemy shall die instantly. One should offer eight thousand oblations of red sesame seeds and *priyaṅgu* grains smeared with ghee. There will be an abundance of wealth and grain. This rite is for all who are devoted to their teacher (*guru*). Two *kanavīra* flowers and two pieces of sandalwood likewise.
Kuṭatva, caṭṭa, and nidra are names for *puṣpadāru* (deodar) and *haridrā* (turmeric); among them, *utpala* refers to the filaments of the lotus (*padma*).
Priyaṅgu, śatapuṣpa, and likewise white siddhārtha; nirguṇḍī, bhūtakeśara, and rocanā.
The three pungents (tṛkaṭuka), the seed of the female monkey (vānarī), realgar (manaḥśilā), the three myrobalans (triphalā), uśīra, neem leaves (nimbapatraka),
the seeds of phalakara, asafoetida (hiṅgu), and marking-nut (bhallātaka).
One should cause these twenty-five parts to be made in equal proportions.
Having combined them with *puṣpāditya* and having combined them with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*),
one should grind them with the five products of the cow.
Having made pills of the desired size, one should dry them in the sun.
Having become intent on fasting, especially on the eighth day of the dark fortnight,
one should recite the Śvetadevatā mantra eight thousand times.
Thus, one should complete [the rite] with the installation-homa according to the previously prescribed method;
one should cause the five—the seat, the plaster, and the head—to be offered for the planets.
At that very moment, one is liberated from all defects; there is no doubt about this.
By applying an ointment on the heads of children, a child is set free. By offering incense during malignant planetary seizures (*duṣṭagraha*), one may bring about liberation.
By applying it as an ointment to the head during all types of fever, one becomes free from fever.
One should wear it on the forehead during an assembly, in a dispute, or at the king’s gate.
A woman should smear it on the ends of her hair; she will bring others under her control.
A maiden who wears it will become fortunate.
One should smear [the vagina] with the substances from the wombs of female animals that give birth to deformed offspring; she will give birth quickly.
In all cases of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), if one drinks [the substance] together with cow’s urine, one becomes healthy.

During the fertile period, if one drinks it together with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for women who have recently given birth, the fetus remains stable and she becomes possessed of a son.
In cases of blood-related colic, one should drink it with rice-water; thus the pain is pacified.
It destroys diseases of the eyes.
At the time of being bitten by a venomous creature, one should apply [the remedy] together with phlegm; thus one becomes free from poison.
It constantly causes lions, tigers, bears, forest trees, *viccha*, date palms, and so forth to abandon all malevolent spirits;
moreover, it always brings about good fortune that is beloved by all people.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, the Exposition on the Application of Medicines, concerning the Expansion of Ritual Actions.
